articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-Related Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 23, 2026.
Further details regarding the specific individuals or entities targeted and the reasons for their designation were made available on the Treasury's website.
These actions are part of ongoing efforts to counter Iran's destabilizing activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran Designations and Cuba FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran designations and issued updated Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) related to Cuba on November 20, 2026.
The Iran designations aim to further pressure the Iranian regime, while the Cuba FAQs provide guidance on existing regulations.
This action reflects the U.S. government's continued focus on both Iran and Cuba sanctions programs.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Counter Narcotics and Cyber Actors, Amends Russia GL
body: OFAC announced new designations targeting counter narcotics and cyber-related activities on November 19, 2026.
In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued an Illicit Drugs General License and an amended Russia-related General License, along with updated Frequently Asked Questions.
These measures aim to disrupt illicit financial networks and provide clarity on authorized transactions related to Russia.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new counter terrorism designations on November 18, 2026.
These designations target individuals and entities involved in supporting terrorist activities globally.
The action underscores the U.S. commitment to combating terrorism financing and disrupting extremist networks.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Actors
body: OFAC announced new designations targeting both counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities on November 13, 2026.
This dual focus highlights the interconnectedness of illicit financial flows supporting both drug trafficking and terrorist organizations.
The designations aim to disrupt these networks and protect the U.S. financial system from abuse.

articles.headline: OFAC Updates Iran Designation Information
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) published an update to its Iran designation information on November 9, 2026.
This update provides additional details or modifications to existing listings related to Iran.
Such updates are routine as OFAC maintains and refines its sanctions lists.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-Related Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 6, 2026.
These actions are part of the ongoing U.S. strategy to exert economic pressure on Iran.
The designations target entities and individuals deemed to be supporting Iran's illicit activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber and Transnational Criminal Organizations, Imposes Cuba Sanctions
body: OFAC announced new designations targeting cyber-related activities and transnational criminal organizations, alongside new Cuba designations, on November 5, 2026.

The Cuba designations were accompanied by the publication of a Cuba-related determination, paving the way for sanctions on the electronics, manufacturing, marine, and technology sectors of the Cuban economy.
These actions underscore the U.S. commitment to disrupting malicious cyber actors, combating organized crime, and increasing pressure on the Cuban government.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran Designations, Updates Listings, Amends Venezuela GL
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and updates to certain Iran-related listings on November 4, 2026.
Concurrently, OFAC published an Iran-related alert and issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and Frequently Asked Question.

Most recently, OFAC issued General License 5AA, further delaying the effectiveness of the authorization in GL 5 until December 18, 2026, impacting transactions related to the PdVSA 2020 8.5 percent bond.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Iran-related General License on October 29, 2026.
General Licenses authorize certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under sanctions programs.
This amendment likely provides specific permissions or clarifications for certain activities involving Iran.

articles.headline: EU Restricts Trade with 15 Entities Linked to Russia's Military-Industrial Complex
body: The Council of the European Union decided on November 25, 2026, to add 15 Russian entities to the list of those subject to tighter export restrictions on dual-use goods and advanced technologies.
These entities are part of Russia's military and industrial complex, or have links with or otherwise support Russia's defense and security sector.
The Council also decided to remove one entity from the list, lifting the export restrictions that applied to it.

articles.headline: EU Designates 12 Individuals and 101 Entities for Undermining Ukraine's Sovereignty
body: On November 16, 2026, the European Union adopted new legal measures, introducing parallel listings of 12 individuals and 101 entities under the sanctions regime concerning actions undermining or threatening the territorial integrity, sovereignty, and independence of Ukraine.
These listings target nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions, as well as individuals and entities in the Russian oil and energy sector.
The measures also include the sole shareholder of Russian retail giant Wildberries and an individual controlling a majority stake in Ozon, a major Russian e-commerce company.

articles.headline: UK Revokes Sanctions on Russian Vessel 'LNG SOARS'
body: On November 20, 2026, the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office updated the UK Sanctions List on GOV.UK with the revocation of sanctions on the vessel 'LNG SOARS'.
A revocation signifies a removal from the list following an official decision-making process.
The 'LNG SOARS' (IMO 9307205) was previously subject to shipping sanctions under The Russia (Sanctions) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019.

articles.headline: UN Security Council Renews Yemen Sanctions, Expands Maritime Oversight
body: The United Nations Security Council unanimously adopted Resolution 2837 (2026) on November 12, 2026, renewing targeted asset freezes and travel bans under the Yemen sanctions regime until November 14, 2027.
The resolution also extends the mandate of the Yemen Panel of Experts until December 15, 2027, and expands the panel from five to six members, introducing dedicated maritime security expertise.
This expansion aims to monitor suspected arms shipments and threats to commercial shipping routes, particularly in the Red Sea, Gulf of Aden, and Bab al-Mandab Strait.
articles.source: UN Meetings Coverage and Press Releases / ZIGRAM

articles.headline: UN Security Council ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List Amended
body: On November 20, 2026, the ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List of individuals and entities was amended.
These amendments followed the 2025 Annual Review conducted in accordance with Security Council resolution 2734 (2024).
Technical amendments were implemented on all entries in the 'Review concluded on' field, with the text '2 Nov. 2026' added.

articles.headline: BIS Imposes New Export Controls on Advanced AI Chips and Remote Access to Data Centers
body: On November 16, 2026, the U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued an interim final rule (IFR) establishing new export controls on advanced computing items, including advanced semiconductors, and certain foreign data center activities involving remote access to computing power.

The rule, effective upon its publication in the Federal Register on November 19, 2026, aims to prevent foreign adversaries from bypassing existing limits on sensitive U.S. technology by running workloads on chips located in other countries, including through rented cloud infrastructure.

Key provisions include a new end-use control for advanced computing items destined for non-U.S. data centers that provide remote access to a 'significant volume of compute power' to end users headquartered in Macau or a Country Group D:5 destination (including China), and new destination-based license requirements for exports to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil.
articles.source: Federal Register / Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom LLP

articles.headline: BIS Adds Seven Entities to Entity List for Diversion Risk
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amended the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by adding seven entities to the Entity List, effective November 23, 2026.

These entities, located in Malaysia (3), Singapore (3), and Thailand (1), were added due to a significant risk of their involvement in diverting advanced computing commodities to unauthorized end uses or end users.
A license is now required for all items subject to the EAR for these entities, and license applications will be reviewed under a presumption of denial.

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
